title: Friends say Memorial Drive police shooting victim was down on his luck
subtitle: Wesley Davidson fell into addiction after a workplace injury and subsequent rejection for workers compensation
article: One of two men who died after Calgary police opened fire on a stolen cube van on Memorial Drive last month has been identified by loved ones as Wesley Davidson, a former oil patch worker remembered as a man with a big heart who unfortunately fell on hard times.
Davidson, 46, and two other men - whose identities have not been revealed- were involved in a low-speed police chase on the morning of May 29.

The men had been reported to police by a security guard at a private property in Mayland Heights and fled the area in a stolen five-ton cube van. At the time, police said the van was driving erratically - having hit a barricade and a building - and multiple officers began tailing the vehicle as it headed down Memorial Drive.

Police said officers attempted to pull the vehicle over and confine it multiple times, but due to "rapidly changing dynamics," an officer - a 13-year member of the force - discharged their firearm. Witnesses told Postmedia they saw police shoot through the driver and passenger windows of the van.
Davidson and one other man died at the scene while another was taken to hospital in police custody.

Jody, a long-time friend of Davidson who requested to be referred to only by his first name, said the man was like a brother to him. Davidson\'s death - and the tragic circumstances surrounding it - has been gutting for people close to him.

"Wes had a big heart, and he didn\'t have much, but if you were in need, he would help you any way he could," said Jody, who attended high school with Davidson in the northern Alberta town of Beaverlodge, located 40 kilometres west of Grande Prairie.

Davidson formerly worked as a well tester in northern Alberta oil fields. But a workplace injury around 2008 that rendered him unable to do his job and an unsuccessful battle with the Workers\' Compensation Board - which his sister, Sheila Davidson, said he was still fighting this year - led him to turn to drugs amid increasingly difficult living conditions.

"He was in and out of addiction. And I think a lot of that had to do with the stress of, you know, not being able to work," said Jody. "I mean, you spend quite a bit of your life working, and then all of a sudden, you get hurt - you have nothing, no backup. As soon as (WCB) says no, that\'s it. You\'re on the streets."
Davidson grew up "everywhere," according to his sister, but was born in Fort McMurray. Sheila said their family frequently moved around Alberta when the two were children.

She said she\'d contacted Calgary police a couple of months before the shooting for a wellness check on her brother after she received a text message from him that was "ridiculously long, ridiculously weird and scary."
"I sent it to the Calgary police, and I said, \'I am afraid for his health and safety.\' Period," she said. "I got no response.
"He was really struggling. Everybody dumped him and everybody ditched him and no one would help him."

She said her brother had several health issues and often found himself in fistfights. She believes her brother had chronic traumatic encephalopathy - a brain disease caused by repeated head injuries - and pushed for the medical examiner to test him for the condition after his death.

"He had multiple, multiple medical issues he did not get help for. I tried," said Sheila, who told Postmedia she formerly worked as a nurse. "I\'d bet my life he had CTE ... That\'s my biggest thing - for public safety and for data purposes, they need to test his brain."

Over the last few years, Davidson had floated around Western Canada. He was in B.C. and returned to Alberta after his mother died in March. Calgary was planned as a stop on his way to see his father and other family members in Eastern Canada in the wake of his mother\'s death.
Despite his struggles with addiction, Davidson was not violent by nature, Jody said.
"That\'s why I don\'t understand why that officer did what he did. I really don\'t," he said.
"I could see him going into a convenience store and maybe stealing a sandwich or a chocolate bar - just being in that situation, right? But he wasn\'t violent; he was just down on his luck."
The police response, Jody said, was excessive. He doesn\'t understand why police resorted to their firearms when there were "so many other options" available.

"From what I\'ve seen, they rolled into the meridian, and the police surrounded them. Then, I don\'t know - cops just opened fire, I guess," said Jody. "Whatever they did, they did not deserve to be shot."

Jody hopes people can be compassionate to his friend, whose addiction led him down an arduous path. Through it all, Jody says Davidson was loved and supported by his friends and family - even if he sometimes didn\'t see it that way.
"He did pull back from a lot of his friends because of his addiction. He didn\'t want to be seen like that," Jody said. "It\'s sad. If you knew him - it\'s sad."

The province\'s police watchdog, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, is investigating CPS\'s response to the incident. Sheila said the agency contacted her for a "mandatory report" immediately following her brother\'s death.
"(They) kept calling. I had to do a mandatory report with ASIRT 20 hours after my brother\'s death," she said, adding officials told her the investigation would take roughly a year.

CPS wouldn\'t confirm the identity of any of the men involved in the shooting as ASIRT is investigating it. The civilian oversight agency told Postmedia it couldn\'t release nor confirm the names of the people involved in the incident per its naming policy.
